issues.legal_issue: An external body cannot dictate the course of a criminal investigation, although it may identify investigative lapses and leave the police to decide what further action is warranted.
material_facts: A commission asked the police to add an offence under the special caste-protection law and submit a supplementary charge sheet.
The supplementary report stated that the additional charge was being submitted at the commission’s direction.
It was unclear whether the commission had conducted an inquiry, and the commission’s procedural rules permitted it to inquire whether an appropriate charge sheet had been filed.
issues.conclusion: The commission could draw investigative shortcomings to the police’s attention, but it could not direct the police to add a charge; the decision on proper or further investigation belonged to the police.
issues.legal_principle: The course of a criminal investigation falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the police; superior police officers may supervise under Section 36 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, while superior courts may monitor in exceptional situations but do not thereby supervise. Under Rule 7.5.2(vi) of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes Rules of Procedure, the Commission could inquire whether a proper charge sheet had been filed, but not dictate the investigation. The Court relied on R. Sarala v. T.S. Velu, (2000) 4 SCC 459, and referred to Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary, (2014) 2 SCC 532.

predicates.criminal_investigation: The matter concerns the conduct of a criminal investigation.
predicates.external_body_directed_specific_charge: An outside body instructed the investigators to add a specific charge rather than merely identify a possible investigative lapse.

issues.definition: When a criminal investigation is concerned and an outside body directed the investigators to add a specific charge, that direction cannot control the investigation.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising inherent jurisdiction may quash a charge or part of a charge sheet without quashing the entire prosecution.
material_facts: The accused sought to challenge only the additional charge in a supplementary report, while the original charges under other offences remained.
The High Court rejected the challenge on the ground that charges could not be quashed piecemeal.
issues.conclusion: There is no legal prohibition on quashing a charge sheet in part; a person may challenge prosecution on particular charges, and the court may intervene only to the extent required by law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, permits the High Court to act to implement orders under the Code, prevent abuse of process, or otherwise secure the ends of justice. The provision does not require a charge sheet to be quashed as a whole when the basis for intervention concerns only particular charges.

predicates.inherent_jurisdiction_quashing_proceedin: The proceeding asks a court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal process.
predicates.challenge_limited_to_particular_charge: The accused challenges prosecution on one or more particular charges rather than the entire prosecution.
predicates.grounds_for_intervention_apply_to_that_c: The legal ground for intervention applies to the challenged charge or charges.

issues.definition: In an inherent-jurisdiction quashing proceeding, when the challenge and its legal basis concern particular charges, the charge sheet may be quashed only in part.

issues.legal_issue: A supplementary charge sheet filed at the direction of an outside body is an abuse of process where the underlying complaint does not allege facts making out the added offence.
material_facts: The original complaint described an assault, abuse and threat but contained no allegation of harassment based on caste.
The first charge sheet proceeded only under the general criminal offences initially reported.
More than two years later, the complainant approached a commission, which requested that the special caste-protection offence be added.
The supplementary report stated that the added charge was submitted at the commission’s direction.
The Court found that the allegations did not make out the ingredients of the added offence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have exercised its inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse of process, and the supplementary report filed at the commission’s direction was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, empowers the High Court to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice. Section 3(1)(x) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, required an intentional insult or intimidation, with intent to humiliate a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, in a place within public view. A charge sheet filed at the dictate of someone other than the police amounts to abuse of process; the Court also applied the principle that investigation is within the police’s exclusive jurisdiction, relying on R. Sarala v. T.S. Velu, (2000) 4 SCC 459.

predicates.inherent_power_quashing_petition: The accused asks a court to use its inherent power to quash criminal process.
predicates.report_at_external_direction: Investigators filed a supplementary report adding a charge because an outside body directed them to do so.
predicates.required_offense_allegation_absent: The complaint contains no allegation establishing an essential element of the added offence.

issues.definition: When an accused seeks inherent-power review, the supplementary report was filed at an outside body’s direction, and the complaint lacks an essential allegation for the added offence, the supplementary report is quashed.
